item.title: Stuck in Orlando for Six Hours, Columbus, Ohio Musician Keith Hanlon Made an Album for Airport Workers
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Columbus, Ohio musician Keith Hanlon made his ambient album Music for Airport Workers during a six-hour Orlando layover.
item.content:encoded:
Keith Hanlon's Music for Airport Workers turns a rerouted flight into an ambient tribute to TSA agents, gate crews and everyone who keeps the terminal running.

Columbus, Ohio musician Keith Hanlon turned a flight delay into a full album. When his airline swapped his direct Columbus-to-New York flight for one with a six-hour layover in Orlando, he found a quiet corner of the terminal and started Music for Airport Workers.

The ambient record came out Sept. 25, 2026, on Argentine label Cyclical Dreams. It is Hanlon's first release for the label.

The man behind the board

Hanlon has been recording electronic, ambient, and post-rock music for more than 20 years. He was a longtime member of the Black Swans. Today he is a producer, recording engineer and co-owner of Secret Studio in Columbus.

The layover that started it

The trip happened last November. Hanlon had been tinkering with generative ambient music that he hadn't quite figured out, and the layover gave him time to dig back in.

He told Matter News the corner he found had one restaurant, no departing flights, and almost nobody around. He started making music about how air travel felt to him, pulling from his own travel memories. Then he began to wonder about the people who work in airports every day: what they want, and what they do when they clock out.

Inside the music

The title is a deliberate nod to Brian Eno's 1979 landmark Ambient 1: Music for Airports, the record often credited with defining ambient music. Hanlon's version swaps the travelers for the workers.

The eight tracks lean on travel scenes:

  • "TSA Dreamer" imagines the inner life of a security agent who watches people leave all day without going anywhere.
  • "On the Air" recalls a Fourth of July flight out of Chicago, watching fireworks below. Low-frequency sounds stand in for the explosions.
  • "Slightly Unsettled" carries the low-grade tension anyone who has sprinted for a gate will recognize.

Another piece reaches for the disorienting perpetual twilight of a summer trip to Iceland.

How he built it

The album started almost by accident. Hanlon used generative software that triggers random MIDI notes, then treated the results like clay: stretching notes, changing keys, and adjusting how often sounds fire before layering more parts on top. Guitar appears on the closing track. Hanlon played and recorded every instrument himself.

The process wasn't always smooth. His first piece came from 45 minutes of generative music he initially disliked. He set it aside, came back later, and salvaged part of it for something new. He says a track is done when it feels like it has created a world of its own.

Why it hits

Most people treat airports as places to escape as fast as possible. Hanlon asks you to slow down and notice the people who never leave. For his question about the TSA agent, he put it simply: "Who are they at their core?"

Where to listen and follow

Stream or buy Music for Airport Workers on Cyclical Dreams' Bandcamp (digital and CD) and explore his catalog at keithhanlon.bandcamp.com.

item.title: 300,000 TikTok Fans, Barely Known at Home: Columbus, Ohio's HummusVacuum Built Its Following Backwards
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Columbus, Ohio pop-punk band HummusVacuum has 300K+ TikTok fans. Meet the band behind debut album The Art of a Fake Laugh.
item.content:encoded:
HummusVacuum started as Kevin Cappy's pandemic screen name. Now it's a three-piece with a debut album on Smartpunk Records and festival dates across the Midwest.

Columbus, Ohio emo-punk band HummusVacuum has more than 300,000 TikTok fans and over 100,000 Instagram followers. Yet when Columbus Underground co-founder Walker Evans asked around town about them earlier this year, almost nobody knew who they were.

Frontman Kevin Cappy has an explanation. He said Columbus Underground is "kind of reverse-engineered." Most bands win their city first and spread outward. HummusVacuum went national online and is only now planting its flag at home.

A screen name that became a band

Cappy grew up in Cleveland. He picked up his first instruments at 10, was playing in touring bands by 19, and played his first show at Peabody's, a scrappy club near Cleveland State's campus. That's where he fell in love with emo and hardcore.

A pandemic-era job loss, plus a long-distance relationship he wanted to close the gap on, brought him to Columbus. Soon after he settled in, he started posting music videos and comedy on TikTok under the username HummusVacuum. It was a COVID project, not a band. The name simply stuck.

Today HummusVacuum is a real lineup: Cappy on lead vocals and guitar, Christian Gehring on drums, and Evan Applefeller on bass and vocals.

Pop-punk with a punchline

The band's Bandcamp sums up the mission as bridging sincerity and humor: big, anthemic power-pop songs mixed with fast, eccentric detours. Live, they write comedy bits between songs that lead into the next tune. Cappy compares the vibe to Bo Burnham with extra caffeine.

The songs can also bite. Tracks like "G-U-I-L-L-O-T-I-N-E" and "Salt & Vinegar" carry pointed political lyrics, and Cappy's short-form videos, some with millions of views, often pair those songs with clips of people he wants to call out. He doesn't consider HummusVacuum a political band, but he won't steer away from what he feels strongly about.

The Art of a Fake Laugh

The debut album, The Art of a Fake Laugh, came out May 22, 2026, on Smartpunk Records, an Orlando, Florida, label that began as an emo-punk blog in the MySpace era. The 11 tracks mix fan favorites that trickled out online with brand-new songs, including "The Claw Is Rigged Anyway," "Whoops! (I Think I Ruined My Life)" and "Lexapro Skater."

Cappy wrote the music and lyrics. Steve Perrino produced and mixed the record, Adam Cichocki mastered it, and Amanda Eiginger made the artwork. A colored-vinyl pressing followed on Aug. 14.

Cappy says the theme is staying light-hearted in a world that often feels dark and finding humor where you least expect it.

Why Columbus matters to them

HummusVacuum spent the summer on the road, playing Jorts Fest in Nashville, Stoopfest and PUG Fest in Michigan, and club dates in Iowa City and Minneapolis. At home, the band saves its Columbus shows for special occasions so it doesn't burn out local fans.

Cappy still loves Cleveland, but he's bullish on his adopted city. He points out that Columbus has roughly double the reliable 100-to-300-capacity venues of Cleveland or Cincinnati.

Where to listen and follow

Stream or buy The Art of a Fake Laugh on Bandcamp and find the band as HummusVacuum on TikTok and Instagram.

item.title: Cleveland, Ohio Guitar Builder Freddy Hill Quit Music for 10 Years to Raise His Son. At 50, He Just Made His First Solo Album
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Cleveland, Ohio guitar builder Freddy Hill took a decade off to raise his son. Now 50, he's released his debut solo album, August.
item.content:encoded:
Freddy Hill went from alt-country sideman to woodworker to weekly jam-night host, then cut August after a single rehearsal.

Cleveland, Ohio singer-songwriter Freddy Hill walked away from music for a decade when his son was born. Now 50, the Stow native has finished August, his first solo album, and celebrated it with a release party at Spotlight Cleveland on Oct. 17.

If you've spent a Wednesday night on Cleveland's near West Side, you may already know him. Hill hosts a weekly jam night at Spotlight and holds a monthly residency at Brothers Lounge. He also builds guitars by hand.

From grunge kid to alt-country road dog

Hill grew up in Stow, a Summit County suburb between Akron and Cleveland. His high school years landed in the middle of the grunge era, and he told Cleveland Scene he was a huge Soundgarden fan. His all-time favorite band, though, is Van Halen.

At Ohio University, he discovered the blues. In the early 2000s, he moved back to Northeast Ohio for grad school at Kent State, befriended singer-songwriter Patrick Sweany and other local players, and then quit school to get serious about music. That run included several years in the alt-country band Roger Hoover and the Whiskeyhounds, which released records and toured the region.

The decade he stepped away

Around the same time, Hill started a woodworking business. He eventually parted ways with the Whiskeyhounds, and when his son arrived, he stopped performing almost entirely. For about 10 years, his only gigs were ukulele sing-alongs for his kid.

The woodworking stuck. Hill works out of the Screw Factory, a Lakewood building full of artists and makers. A segment on Ideastream's Applause followed his move from furniture to building acoustic guitars there.

The jam night that pulled him back

In 2017, Ryan Foltz of Cleveland Audio talked Hill into signing up for Lottery League, the local event that randomly pairs musicians into new bands. A bandmate from that project, Jess Horvath, then introduced him to Cleveland's jam-night circuit.

Hill told Cleveland Scene the jam scene "changed my life." He rediscovered the guitar, started writing again, and within a few years was running a jam night of his own.

How August got made

Hill wrote about 20 songs, aiming to record 10. He rehearsed once with drummer Mic Fox, then headed to Dark Current, the studio run by local musician and producer John Panza.

The result, per Cleveland Scene, sounds like 1950s Chess Records blues filtered through a modern rock lens: loose, woozy and live-sounding. Hill admits the record sounds like two guys who rehearsed the night before, and says he's proud of it anyway. He hopes there's enough interest to justify a second album, because he wants back in the studio.

Why it hits

Hill's story isn't about chasing fame at 50. It's about a working craftsman who set music down for family, found his way back through community, and made the record anyway. For anyone who ever shelved a passion, August is proof the door stays open.

Where to listen and follow

Catch Hill live at Spotlight Cleveland's Wednesday jam night (spotlightcle.com) or his monthly Brothers Lounge residency.

item.title: Cleveland, Ohio's Violet Ray Wrote a Song About Tony Hawk, and It Drops on Halloween
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Cleveland, Ohio skate-punk band Violet Ray drops Skate Gang on Halloween, with a Tony Hawk tribute and a Lakewood release show Oct. 23.
item.content:encoded:
Violet Ray's new album Skate Gang adds metal, funk and synths to its skate-punk attack. The band throws its release party Friday in Lakewood.

Cleveland, Ohio punk band Violet Ray writes songs about skateboarding, by skateboarders, for skateboarders, and its new album has a track about Tony Hawk. Skate Gang arrives on all major platforms on Halloween, Oct. 31, with a release show this Friday, Oct. 23, at the Five O'Clock Lounge in Lakewood.

The band has leaned so hard into skate culture that local musician Nick Wolff and his band Gemini Lounge started calling them the Kings of Skate Rock. The nickname stuck, and Violet Ray now prints it on its flyers and merch.

A '90s punk lifer on a board since 1988

Frontman Billy Somerville has been skating since 1988. Before Violet Ray, he sang in the Hooligans, a popular Cleveland punk band that split in 2000. He started Violet Ray in 2017, originally as a politically charged band.

That changed on the band's first full-length album, This Is Skate Rock. Every song referenced skating in some way, from skate legends to wipeout slang. Somerville told Cleveland Scene he once drove all the way to Portland, Oregon, just to skate the Burnside Skate Park.

The skate rock sound has stuck ever since. At the time of that debut, the lineup was Somerville on vocals and guitar, Mike Layton on lead guitar, Rich Kauffman on bass, and Eric Riehm on drums.

What's new on Skate Gang

The new album pulls from songs written as far back as 2020 and as recently as last year. Somerville says the band has been breaking away from its punk roots, borrowing from early Iron Maiden on the metal side and Austin skate-rock band the Big Boys on the funk side.

The biggest surprise is synthesizers. They show up on "Birdman," the band's ode to Tony Hawk, the world's most famous skateboarder.

Another standout is "Ripper Girl," a snotty, NOFX-style track written for Abby, a young skater who rode with Somerville's crew. He remembers her as one of the toughest skaters he's known. She once broke her tailbone snowboarding and never complained. The song pushes back on people who dismiss female skaters. Somerville's line on it is simple: let the skateboarding do the talking.

A skate band on a surf label

Skate Gang comes out on Otitis Media Records, a Corpus Christi, Texas, label run by Christopher Puryear. Somerville says Violet Ray is the only skate-rock band on what is mostly a surf-rock label. The band talked to other punk labels around the country, but none felt like a fit.

Otitis gave the band full creative control and time to finish the record. That mattered, because Somerville was recovering from a diabetic coma that he says nearly killed him while the album came together.

Why it hits

Skate punk has always been about community: the crew at the park, the scabbed knees, the songs blasting from somebody's car. Violet Ray isn't chasing a trend. It's keeping a Cleveland tradition alive, now with a little more range.

Where to listen and follow

Stream earlier releases on Bandcamp and follow Violet Ray on Facebook for the Oct. 31 drop.

item.title: New York Songwriter Anjoli Simone's Entire Bio Is One Deadpan Line. Now BIRP! Is Playing 'Inside Voice'
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Who is Anjoli Simone? Meet the New York singer-songwriter and guitarist behind 'Inside Voice,' now featured on BIRP!'s October 2026 indie playlist.
item.content:encoded:
A New York guitarist with a dry sense of humor, now featured on BIRP!'s October 2026 indie playlist. Here's what to know.

Not every artist wants to tell you their whole life story. Anjoli Simone, a singer-songwriter based in New York, N.Y., keeps it short and funny and lets the music do the talking. Her song "Inside Voice" just landed on BIRP!'s October 2026 Indie Pop / Rock playlist, so here's a quick guide to the songwriter behind it.

Who Is Anjoli Simone?

Anjoli Simone is a singer-songwriter and guitarist based in New York, according to her Spotify bio. The rest of that bio is a single, deadpan line: she's been kind of walking around and looking around for over two decades.

It's a refreshing change from the usual wall of buzzwords artist bios tend to lean on, and it reads like the line of someone who notices things.

About "Inside Voice"

"Inside Voice" was released on August 2, 2024, through Sad Passions, and runs just over three minutes. As of now, it has more than 6,600 plays on Spotify.

The title itself is a phrase most of us heard as kids: use your inside voice. It's the reminder to keep it down, stay polite, and not take up too much space. That makes it a clever title for a singer-songwriter release, since songwriting is often about saying out loud the things we usually keep quiet.

Why the BIRP! Playlist Matters

Anjoli Simone's music is currently featured on BIRP!'s Indie Pop / Rock playlist for October 2026, according to her Spotify profile. BIRP! is an indie music discovery outlet that publishes monthly playlists of the best new indie tracks it finds, with the full lists at birp.fm.

For an emerging artist, that kind of curation is valuable. Editorial playlists from respected tastemakers put songs in front of listeners actively hunting for new music, and they often signal early that an artist is worth watching.

The Singer-Songwriter Tradition

Quick context for newer listeners: the singer-songwriter tradition puts the writer and their perspective front and center, usually with an instrument like guitar or piano anchoring the song. New York has a deep history here, from the 1960s Greenwich Village folk scene to the anti-folk movement at the Sidewalk Cafe in the 1990s and 2000s. Anjoli Simone joins the city's long line of songwriters, guitar in hand and something to say.

Why You Should Listen

With around 550 monthly listeners on Spotify, Anjoli Simone is still a true discovery. That's the fun part: you get to hear an artist before the bigger playlists catch up, and "Inside Voice" is a great first step.

Where to Listen

Stream "Inside Voice" on Anjoli Simone's Spotify page.

item.title: Who Is RILA? The Bulgarian-French Voice Behind 'Life Soldiers'
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Who is RILA? Meet the singer from Bulgaria's mountains, now based in France, behind 'Life Soldiers,' who has shared a festival stage with ZAZ.
item.content:encoded:
Spotted at 16, from a small town in the Bulgarian mountains and now based in France, RILA is building a cinematic pop world.

Some artists have a story that sounds like a movie opening. RILA is one of them: a singer from a small town in the Bulgarian mountains who was spotted as a teenager for her voice and is now making cinematic pop in France. Her song "Life Soldiers" started the project.

Who Is RILA?

According to her Spotify biography, RILA comes from a small town in the Bulgarian mountains and is now based in France. She found comfort in singing from a young age, and her artistic identity grew out of what her bio calls a profound quest for meaning. She channels her Franco-Bulgarian heritage into her sound.

At 16, she was spotted for her distinctive voice, and her bio says she has since appeared on MCM, Virgin Radio, Clubbing TV, and Bulgarian national TV channels BTV and BNT.

The Sound

RILA describes her music as cinematic, with heartfelt pop melodies. Her bio says it carries the emotional depth of artists like Adele, Agnes Obel and Lana Del Rey, and that she draws from spirituality and the natural world.

Her songs focus on human relationships and life's highs and lows, especially moments of reflection, perseverance, and stillness. If you love emotional, atmospheric pop with a sense of space, that's the lane she's working in.

About "Life Soldiers"

"Life Soldiers" launched the RILA project in 2024. Her bio calls it her first single, and the track runs just under four minutes. The title alone fits her stated themes: perseverance and pushing through life's ups and downs.

Since that debut, RILA has released five singles, according to her bio. That's steady output for a project that only launched recently.

A Big Festival Moment

In June 2025, RILA performed at Bulgaria's Francofolies Festival. Her bio says she shared the stage with French, Bulgarian, and international artists, including ZAZ, Alexandra Stan, and KRISKO. For a newer artist, sharing a lineup with names like that is a serious milestone.

What's Next

RILA is opening a new chapter by releasing her first French-language songs, starting with "La Lune." According to her bio, the track blends modern pop production with subtle touches of traditional Bulgarian folk, a natural next step for an artist built on two cultures.

Why She's One to Watch

RILA has the pieces that tend to add up: a distinctive voice, a clear identity rooted in two countries, and early TV, radio, and festival exposure. "Life Soldiers" is where it all started, and it's a great place for you to start, too.

Where to Listen

Stream "Life Soldiers" and her newer singles on RILA's Spotify page.

item.title: What's Haunting Keeymo? Inside 'Haunted Houses,' the Halloween Project Born on House Arrest
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Keeymo's 'Haunted Houses' drops Oct. 31 via Authentic Empire and Tha Lights Global. Here's the story behind the Toronto-based rapper's Halloween project.
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina-raised, Toronto-based artist turns a year tied to the house into a late-night-drive project, out Oct. 31 via Authentic Empire and Tha Lights Global.

Some projects are named for the season. Keeymo's "Haunted Houses" just happens to fit. The Carolina-raised, Toronto-based artist is dropping the project on all platforms on Halloween, Oct. 31, and the title comes from a much more personal place than costumes and candy.

Who Is Keeymo?

Keeymo started his music journey in 2017 while he was still living in Carolina. He moved to Toronto right before the COVID-19 pandemic, and that's when he fully locked in.

The years that followed were less about dropping songs and more about finding his lane. He spent that time figuring out his approach instead of putting out music, then revamped his artistry and left behind his earlier name, Kan Boy. Now, he says, he's here to stay.

The Story Behind "Haunted Houses"

"Haunted Houses" reflects the past year of Keeymo's life. He spent that stretch on house arrest, and being confined at home pushed him to reflect even further back on his life, where he says he noticed a lot of things others didn't.

That's where the title comes from. Being tied to the house, he explains, "it can get dark and lonely, kinda like a 'Haunted House.'"

Despite the heavy inspiration, the project was built for motion. Keeymo says he made the mood for late-night drives, a vibe that runs through "Ghost Town."

The Sound and the Credits

Keeymo's main producer and engineer, EA, gave each song on "Haunted Houses" its final touches. The tracks "MPO" and "Bobby Jones" feature Keeymo under his former alias, Kan Boy, a nod to the era before the revamp.

One standout bar comes from "Toronto" / "Ghost Town": "She's always with her work friends, I'm always with my church friends." Keeymo says the line is about trying to make it work with a girl who was always working against him.

The cover art leans all the way into the title: dripping orange lettering over a black-and-white photo of a house, framed by archival-style protest signs and newspaper headlines about housing discrimination.

Release Details

Artist: Keeymo

Project: "Haunted Houses"

Release date: Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026

Label: Authentic Empire

Distribution: Tha Lights Global

Producer and engineer: EA

Pre-save: tlg.vyd.co/HauntedHouses

Follow Keeymo

Keeymo goes by KeeymoSlimeee on Instagram and TikTok. Find all of his links on Linktree, and pre-save "Haunted Houses" before it drops on Halloween.

item.title: Who Is Irène Schrader? The Singer Mixing Mandopop and French Chanson
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Who is Irène Schrader? Meet the Paris-based multilingual singer-songwriter behind 'Ladida,' blending Mandopop, French chanson and modern electro-pop.
item.content:encoded:
Raised between cultures, writing in English, French and Mandarin, and now based in Paris. Meet the artist behind 'Ladida.'

What happens when you grow up between cultures and fall in love with music from all of them? You get Irène Schrader. The multilingual singer-songwriter blends Mandopop, French chanson and modern electro-pop, and her song "Ladida" is an easy way to step into her world.

Who Is Irène Schrader?

According to a February 2026 episode description on the podcast hosted at damyankee.podbean.com, Irène Schrader is now based in Paris after previously living in Amsterdam, where she experienced the city's electronic music scene. The same description calls her a "Third Culture Kid," a term for people raised in cultures different from their parents' or passport country's.

Her childhood was truly international. Per that podcast description, she played classical piano as a child in China and lived in Shanghai, where she discovered hybrid styles like Shanghai jazz. She writes music in English, French and Mandarin, and counts French icon Françoise Hardy and Mandarin pop among her influences.

Her Spotify bio adds a charming detail: music is her constant companion, and she composes wherever she happens to be, whether in her room, on a train or in the air.

Mandopop Meets Chanson: A Quick Guide

Irène's bio says her sound draws on 1970s and '90s Mandopop and late-'60s and '70s French chanson, plus modern electro-pop and indie. Here's what those mean:

  • Mandopop is Mandarin-language pop music. Its '70s era produced legends like Teresa Teng, while the '90s brought a polished boom of ballads and pop across Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China.
  • French chanson is a lyric-driven style of French song. Its late-'60s and '70s era, home to artists like Françoise Hardy and Serge Gainsbourg, is famous for cool, intimate vocals and elegant arrangements.

Both traditions prize melody and mood, which makes them natural partners.

About "Ladida"

"Ladida" was released on September 9, 2022, and runs about three and a half minutes. At the time of writing, it has passed 5,500 plays on Spotify. The title has the carefree, sing-song feel of a melody hummed under your breath, a fitting match for an artist who says she writes songs on the go.

Beyond Music

Irène's creative life extends beyond songwriting. The podcast description notes she has also worked in modeling and brand management, and that a production workshop at the 2023 Amsterdam Dance Event boosted her confidence as a producer. Her latest release mentioned there is the EP Eclipse.

Where to Listen

Stream "Ladida" on Irène Schrader's Spotify page, then check out Eclipse.

item.title: What Is War Honey's 'Even Sleep Is Exhausting' Really About?
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: What is War Honey's 'Even Sleep Is Exhausting' about? We break down the Brooklyn band's lockdown-era song from their debut EP 'Shard to Shatter.'
item.content:encoded:
A Brooklyn band, a lockdown-era debut, a song about defending your focus and one of the funniest bios on Spotify.

Ever been so tired that even sleeping feels like work? Brooklyn band War Honey turned that feeling into a song, and it's racked up more than 68,000 Spotify plays. Here's what "Even Sleep Is Exhausting" is about and the story of the band behind it.

Who Are War Honey?

War Honey is an indie rock band from Brooklyn, New York. According to a 2022 review on Here Comes the Flood, the lineup is Gabrielle Dana on vocals and guitar, Ben Fitts on guitar, David Bloom on bass, and Ian Ackerman on drums.

Their sound is hard to pin down, in the best way. Here Comes the Flood described it as art pop with a touch of opera mixed with psychedelic rock. A Grrrl's Two Sound Cents called their debut EP "operatic polemics."

Bonus points for personality: the band's Spotify bio openly mocks the music industry habit of writing glowing third-person bios and passing them off as a stranger's opinion. Then it spirals into an absurd tale about a hat-ruled dimension. It's worth a read.

A Debut Made in Lockdown

War Honey's debut EP, Shard to Shatter, was recorded during the 2020 lockdown, according to A Grrrl's Two Sound Cents, which also reported that the band rented a place in rural Pennsylvania during the pandemic to work on new material. Handstand Records picked up the EP for distribution in 2021.

The pandemic also reshaped the band. Here Comes the Flood reported that their previous bassist and drummer left during that time, and Dana and Fitts rebuilt the group.

What Is "Even Sleep Is Exhausting" About?

"Even Sleep Is Exhausting" appears on Shard to Shatter, with a Spotify release date of December 1, 2020.

The lyrics paint a picture of being under siege. The narrator describes invaders raging around their fortress and breaking in to steal their focus, yet they insist they don't notice. Later, enemies wait on the brink of war, and the narrator repeats that they're unaware.

Read alongside the title, the song captures a very specific kind of exhaustion: being surrounded by stress and conflict while trying to block it out. Pretending not to notice takes energy, too, so even rest stops feeling restful. Released in December 2020, at the end of a stressful year, it's easy to see why the feeling connects.

What Came Next

War Honey followed up with a second EP, Last Woman Left at the Market, in May 2022, and the single "I Don't Blame the Rats" in 2023, according to The Bad Copy.

Where to Listen

Stream "Even Sleep Is Exhausting" on War Honey's Spotify page.

item.title: Who Is Stephanie Hayden? Alberta's Genre-Defying Voice Explained
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Who is Stephanie Hayden? Meet the Alberta, Canada singer-songwriter behind 'Don't want you to leave' from her 2024 album 'Split.'
item.content:encoded:
A track from her album 'Split' is nearing 20,000 streams. Here's your introduction to the Canadian artist.

Alberta might be better known for the Rockies than for its music scene, but Stephanie Hayden is out to change that. Her track "Don't want you to leave" is nearing 20,000 Spotify plays, and it's a strong introduction to a musician who refuses to stick to one genre.

Who Is Stephanie Hayden?

Stephanie Hayden is a musician, singer, and songwriter from Alberta, Canada. Her Spotify biography describes her as a voice that crosses typical genre lines, blending diverse musical influences into a sound that is entirely her own.

Her bio puts connection at the center of her work. She aims to reach people through heartfelt lyrics and melodies, and to make a meaningful difference in her listeners' lives. It also highlights her versatility and emotional performances, describing her music as an immersive experience.

About "Don't want you to leave"

"Don't want you to leave" appears on Stephanie's album Split, released on April 26, 2024. The track runs just over three minutes.

As of this writing, "Don't want you to leave" has more than 19,000 plays on Spotify, and Stephanie has more than 1,800 monthly listeners. For an independent artist, those numbers are encouraging.

The title says a lot on its own. "Don't want you to leave" is a plain, honest sentence, the kind of admission that you need someone to stay. It fits neatly with the heartfelt approach her bio describes.

What "Genre-Defying" Actually Means

You'll see "genre-defying" in plenty of artist bios, so here's what it means in practice. Today's listeners rarely stick to one style. Streaming made it easy to jump from pop to folk to R&B in one playlist, and many artists write the same way, borrowing elements from different genres instead of following one rulebook. For a songwriter focused on emotion, that freedom is a feature, not a bug: the feeling comes first, and the genre follows.

The Canadian Connection

Stephanie comes from a province with real musical pedigree. Alberta has produced acts like k.d. lang and Tegan and Sara, proof that the prairies can launch voices the whole world hears.

Why You Should Listen

item.title: Zippy Raises $20 Million to Modernize the Most Overlooked Corner of the American Housing Market
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Zippy raises a $20M Series C from Saluda Grade to expand manufactured housing loans beyond 27 states and launch new products for communities and retailers.
item.content:encoded:
The manufactured-home lender's Series C from Saluda Grade follows more than $600 million in capital commitments secured this year.

Manufactured homes are one of the last truly affordable paths to owning a home in America. Financing them, however, has long been slow, paper-heavy and underserved by mainstream lenders. Zippy has just raised $20 million to change that.

The tech-enabled lender and loan servicer closed a Series C round with Saluda Grade as the sole investor, committing through its growth equity strategy, FinTech Global reported. Beyond capital, Saluda Grade will support Zippy on credit, capital markets, balance sheet management and product development.

A Lender Built for One Kind of Home

Founded in 2021, Zippy focuses exclusively on manufactured housing finance. It works with manufactured housing communities, retailers, dealers and wholesale partners, and has built its own loan origination platform covering digital applications, partner tools, underwriting, standardized paperwork and data infrastructure.

"Manufactured housing is already one of the most compelling affordable homeownership solutions in America, but it needs a financing system that is just as modern and efficient as the homes themselves," co-founder and CEO Ben Halliday said.

The Numbers Behind the Round

Zippy currently operates in 27 states. In 2026 alone, it has secured more than $600 million in capital commitments, the lending capacity that lets it fund loans at scale. The new equity gives the company room to keep growing that balance sheet while investing in technology.

"Zippy has built an impressive platform in one of the most overlooked sectors of housing finance," said John Stepp, head of ventures at Saluda Grade.

Why Manufactured Housing Is Having a Moment

With home prices and mortgage rates squeezing first-time buyers, manufactured homes offer a far lower entry price than site-built houses. Yet buyers often face higher rates and fewer lending options, in part because many manufactured homes are financed as personal property rather than traditional real estate. Lenders that can underwrite these loans efficiently stand to capture a market that big banks have largely ignored.

That gap is the opportunity Zippy is targeting: a vertical, software-driven lender that understands the economics of manufactured home communities and dealers better than generalist mortgage shops.

Saluda Grade's involvement is also strategic. The firm is known for its work in residential credit and capital markets, expertise that matters for a lender whose growth depends on reliably funding and selling loans. A sole-investor round from a specialist backer suggests conviction in Zippy's underwriting, not just its software.

For buyers, the promise is simple: faster approvals, clearer paperwork and fewer dead ends at the dealership or community office. For the industry, a well-capitalized digital lender could add competition to a segment where options have historically been thin.

What Comes Next

Zippy says the funding will help it expand beyond its current 27-state footprint, launch new loan products through community, retail and wholesale channels, and build out its technology and balance sheet capacity.

If it succeeds, Zippy could help make one of America's most affordable housing options easier to finance, and turn a long-neglected corner of lending into a serious fintech category.

item.title: Affinity Labs Raises $2 Million to Turn Influencers Into Software Founders With AI
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: London's Affinity Labs raises $2M pre-seed led by Fuel Ventures to co-found AI-powered software brands with creators, plus a £497K Innovate UK grant.
item.content:encoded:
The London startup co-founds apps with creators like Olivia Bowen, and says its portfolio revenue has been doubling month over month.

Creators have mastered attention. What most of them have not built is a business that runs without them on camera. London startup Affinity Labs wants to fix that by co-founding software companies with creators, and it just raised $2 million to scale the idea.

The pre-seed round was led by Fuel Ventures, with Antler co-investing, Tech.eu reported. Angel investors from Google DeepMind, Meta and Playfair VC joined, along with creator Marcello Ascani and Kyra CEO Devran Amaratunga Karaca. Affinity Labs also secured a £497,787 grant from Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation.

Creators as Co-Founders

The model is simple to explain and hard to execute. Every product Affinity Labs launches is co-founded with a creator who brings an existing, engaged audience. Affinity Labs supplies the technology, product and operations needed to turn that audience into a paying software brand.

"Creators are the most underleveraged founders in the world," CEO Edoardo Ricci said. "Affinity Labs exists to be that infrastructure, we co-found every product with a leading creator."

Ricci runs the company alongside COO Ahmed Eltom and CTO Sunny Panchal.

AI Does the Heavy Lifting

What makes the approach scalable is a proprietary AI-powered development system that automates stages of the product lifecycle, from identifying software ideas and matching them with creator partners to building, operating and growing the products. That automation is what lets a small team run a portfolio rather than a single app.

Early Traction

Affinity Labs has launched four creator-led brands so far. Interior Design Clinic, built with Olivia Bowen, reached No. 34 in the App Store's Lifestyle category. Archives, built with Basel Ghazoghli, has more than 75,000 users and ranks among the top 200 Education apps. According to the company, portfolio revenue has averaged 100% month-over-month growth over the past three months, meaning it has roughly doubled each month.

Why It Matters

The creator economy has largely monetized through brand deals, merch and consumer products like beverages and cosmetics. Software is a different animal: higher margins, recurring revenue and products that can grow even when the creator takes a break. If AI lowers the cost of building apps far enough, a creator's audience may become the most valuable distribution channel a new software company can have.

What's Next

Affinity Labs will use the funding to expand its portfolio, support existing products and grow its product, growth and engineering teams. Part of the capital, including the Innovate UK grant, will go toward its AI product development technology.

The company plans to launch its first products with U.S. creators in late 2026 and has set an ambitious target of more than 200 creator-led software brands by 2030. For American influencers wondering what comes after the sponsorship era, that could make Affinity Labs a name worth knowing.

item.title: Elevation Capital Bets $10.5 Million That an AI-Powered Indian Studio Can Build Your Next Phone Game Obsession
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Spill Games raises $10.5M Series A led by Elevation Capital to scale its AI-led mobile game studio, Compass engine and casual puzzle titles worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru's Spill Games, maker of Cozy Finds and Zen Math Crossword, lands a Series A roughly six months after its seed round.

The next puzzle game eating up your commute may be coming out of Bengaluru, and it may have been tested, tuned and scaled with help from AI. Spill Games, a two-year-old mobile studio, has raised $10.5 million (about ₹100 crore) in a Series A round led by Elevation Capital.

Existing investors Centre Court Capital and PeerCapital also joined the round, Inc42 reported. The raise comes roughly six months after Spill closed a $3.1 million seed round in April, a fast follow-on that signals strong early traction.

An AI-Led, Portfolio-Driven Studio

Founded in 2024 by Om Misra, Tapan Ranjan and Harsh Garg, Spill builds free-to-play casual, puzzle and hybrid-casual titles for a global audience. Its portfolio includes Cozy Finds, Sticker by Number, Zen Math Crossword, Bird Rescue Jam and Grill Master, monetized through advertising and in-app purchases.

"We started Spill because we love making and playing games," Misra told DealStreetAsia. The business model, however, is built on discipline rather than passion alone. Spill launches games quickly to test assumptions, then uses player feedback and in-game data to decide which titles deserve more investment and which get cut.

The Compass Engine

At the center of that process is Compass, Spill's in-house engine that brings together tools for analytics, player retention, monetization and live operations. Because the infrastructure is reused across games, the studio says it can shorten development and testing cycles, targeting speeds roughly four times faster than traditional approaches.

That speed matters in casual mobile gaming, where hits are unpredictable and user acquisition costs can sink a studio that bets too heavily on any single title.

Built in India, Played in America

Spill is part of a new wave of Indian studios building for players overseas. At the time of its seed round, the company said about half of its users came from the United States, followed by Brazil and Japan. It previously set goals of testing more than 20 prototypes within 18 months and launching five to ten profitable titles.

The timing is notable. India's government has banned real-money gaming, pushing investor attention toward studios that earn money from ads and in-app purchases instead of wagers. Spill sits squarely in that safer lane.

Where the Money Goes

Spill plans to use the new capital to scale its existing games, expand its development pipeline, strengthen the AI and technology capabilities of Compass, acquire users and selectively grow its team.

For Elevation Capital, one of India's most active early-stage firms, the bet is that a data-driven studio can turn hit-making from luck into a repeatable system. If Spill pulls that off, the American players already making up half its audience will be the ones who notice first.

item.title: 5 Things to Know Before You Buy Rapid Rewards Points
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Before you buy Southwest Rapid Rewards points, learn five facts on pricing, real value, Companion Pass rules, limits, and cancellations.
item.content:encoded:
Southwest's points work differently from every other airline's. Five facts decide whether buying them helps you.

Disclosure: YourInfoDaily may earn a commission if you buy through links in this article. Offers change and are often targeted, so confirm the terms in your own account before buying.

Before you buy Rapid Rewards points, know these five things: your discount is personal, a point is worth about 1.3 cents, bought points don't count toward the Companion Pass, the purchase isn't airfare to your card, and point bookings are unusually easy to cancel. Together, they tell you when buying helps and when it doesn't.

1. Your discount is not the same as everyone else's

Southwest's standard price is 3 cents per point. It discounts points regularly, but not equally. One Mile at a Time reported that during a sale running September 2 to October 2, 2026, different members were offered 35%, 45%, or 50% off. Award Travel Finder's tracker, updated October 9, 2026, listed a 50% discount through October 29.

On a purchase of 60,000 points, those tiers look like this:

  • 50% off: $900, or 1.5 cents per point.
  • 45% off: $990, or 1.65 cents per point.
  • 35% off: $1,170, or 1.95 cents per point.

The discount in that sale applied only to purchases of at least 3,000 points in one transaction.

What to do: log in and look at your own offer before you read anyone's verdict on the sale, including this one. A 50% offer and a 35% offer lead to different answers.

2. A point is worth about 1.3 cents, almost every time

With most airlines, a point's value swings widely, and experts hunt for sweet spots. Southwest is different. Frequent Miler explains that award prices depend on demand and the flight's cash price, rising and falling with the fare. Any seat for sale can be booked with points.

The result is predictable value. Frequent Miler's benchmark is 1.3 cents per point. One Mile at a Time estimates 1.1 to 1.5 cents.

That predictability works against buyers. No hidden jackpot makes points bought at 1.5 cents suddenly worth 4 cents. One Mile at a Time concludes that buying at 1.5 cents or more rarely makes sense, because points usually redeem for less.

What to do: treat buying as a way to complete a booking, not as a discount on travel.

3. Bought points do not count toward the Companion Pass

The Companion Pass lets a named companion fly with you for only the taxes. Frequent Miler requires 135,000 qualifying points in a calendar year.

Purchased points do not qualify. Neither do points transferred from another member, most bonus points, or points transferred in from hotel partners or Chase Ultimate Rewards. What does count: base points from paid flights, Southwest credit card spending, card welcome bonuses, and many partner activities.

What to do: if the pass is your target, put your money into paid flights and card spending. Buy points only for redemptions.

See the Rapid Rewards offer on your account.

4. There are limits, and your card sees a different merchant

According to One Mile at a Time, you can buy up to 60,000 points per day, with no annual limit. That is unusually open. Most programs cap purchases annually.

The sale is processed by Points.com, not by Southwest. Your credit card will not record it as an airline purchase, so do not expect an airfare bonus category to apply. One Mile at a Time suggests using a card with a minimum spending requirement or one with strong everyday rewards.

What to do: choose a card for its base earning rate, and buy only what your booking needs. The lack of an annual cap isn't a reason to stock up.

5. Points bookings are easy to undo, and points never expire

This is the best argument for holding Rapid Rewards points at all.

  • Cancellations. Frequent Miler notes that you can cancel award flights for no fee up to 10 minutes before departure, with points returned immediately. One Mile at a Time adds that a canceled cash ticket becomes a travel credit for a future flight, while redeposited points can be used for anyone.
  • Changes. If your flight price drops after you book, Frequent Miler says changing to a cheaper fare returns the difference in points.
  • Expiration. Rapid Rewards points do not expire, and no activity is needed to keep them. Closing your account forfeits them.

What to do: if your travel dates are uncertain, a points booking gives you a clean exit. After you book, check the price again periodically. If it falls, rebook and collect the difference.

Top up your Rapid Rewards balance.

So when should you buy?

  • Buy when you are a few thousand points short of a flight you are ready to book. A 3,000-point top-up at 50% off costs about $45.
  • Consider buying when your plans may change, and you value getting points back more than holding a travel credit.
  • Do not buy to pay for a whole trip at a 35% or 45% discount, to chase the Companion Pass, or because a sale is ending. Another sale will follow.

A quick self-check

  • What discount does my account show?
  • What is the cash fare, and what is the points price?
  • How many points am I actually missing?
  • If I cancel, would I rather hold points or a travel credit?

Two more notes. Southwest offers a Cash + Points option, which Frequent Miler says yields poor value per point. And free checked bags now depend on your fare, elite status, or a Southwest credit card, so include bag costs when you compare a Southwest fare with a competitor's.

FAQ

How much are Rapid Rewards points worth?

About 1.3 cents each by Frequent Miler's benchmark, with a typical range of 1.1 to 1.5 cents.

Is there a limit on how many Southwest points you can buy?

Up to 60,000 per day, with no annual cap.

Do Rapid Rewards points expire?

No.

Can I get a refund on points I buy?

Treat purchases as final and read the terms shown at checkout before you pay.

item.title: Vinci Pharmaceuticals Closes $8M Series A for Needle-Free Retinal Drug Implant
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Vinci Pharmaceuticals closed an $8M+ Series A led by Dynagrow Capital to advance EPIPLANT, a sustained-release episcleral implant for retinal disease, toward a 2027 trial.
item.content:encoded:
The New Jersey eye care company is preparing its EPIPLANT implant for a first-in-human trial in 2027 as an alternative to repeated eye injections.

Vinci Pharmaceuticals, a specialty eye care company based in Avon-by-the-Sea, New Jersey, has closed a Series A financing of more than $8 million to advance its EPIPLANT drug delivery platform. Dynagrow Capital led the round, with support from MintPharma Capital.

The raise follows $8.5 million in seed financing, bringing Vinci's total funding to more than $16.5 million.

What EPIPLANT Is

Many of the most common treatments for retinal diseases, including those affecting the macula, are delivered by injection directly into the eye, often every month or two. The treatment burden is heavy, and many patients stop treatment early, which can lead to vision loss.

EPIPLANT is designed to avoid that. It is a bioerodible implant placed on the outer surface of the eye, against the sclera, that releases medication to the retinal tissues over time without injections into the eye. The platform can currently deliver small-molecule drugs and is designed to work with a range of active ingredients.

The technology was developed in the lab of retina specialist Karl Csaky, MD, PhD, and is licensed from the Retina Foundation of the Southwest in Dallas. Vinci says it holds multiple granted patents and has completed preliminary preclinical testing.

How the Money Will Be Used

The proceeds will fund manufacturing, testing and release of its lead product, EPIPLANT VCI-002, under good manufacturing practice standards, as well as a planned Phase 1/2a first-in-human clinical trial in 2027.

Co-founder, chairman and CEO Philip A. Gioia described the financing as an important step toward that first human study. Dynagrow Capital managing director Sarah Hassan said a needle-free option could help reduce the high dropout rates caused by the burden of current treatment.

Why It Matters

Retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular edema are among the leading causes of vision loss, and the drugs used to treat them form one of the largest markets in ophthalmology. Much of the industry's recent innovation has focused on making treatments last longer between injections.

Vinci is aiming further, removing the intraocular injection entirely. The approach still has to show in humans that it can deliver enough drug to the retina safely and consistently. With the Series A closed, the company has funding to manufacture clinical supply and bring EPIPLANT to its first patients.

item.title: What Is Atlas Atomics? Ramaswamy's $1.9B Nuclear Bet
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Atlas Atomics is the stealth nuclear startup co-founded by Vivek Ramaswamy. It raised about $400M at a $1.9B valuation to build a heavy water reactor.
item.content:encoded:
The stealth company raised about $400M in a General Catalyst-led Series A to build a heavy water reactor that does not need enriched uranium.

Atlas Atomics, a stealth nuclear energy startup co-founded and backed by Vivek Ramaswamy, has raised about $400 million in a Series A round at a valuation of roughly $1.9 billion, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

General Catalyst is leading the round, with Andreessen Horowitz participating. Atlas Atomics, General Catalyst and a16z declined to comment, so the terms have not been confirmed by the company.

Who Is Behind Atlas Atomics

Ramaswamy, the entrepreneur and Ohio gubernatorial candidate, is a co-founder and backer. Day-to-day leadership sits with co-founder Kevin Gan, who spent more than 15 years investing in energy companies, most recently at hedge fund Millennium and before that at D.E. Shaw & Co.

The company's chief nuclear officer is Balendra Sutharshan, a former chief operating officer of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Department of Energy's largest science and energy lab and a central institution in American nuclear research. VentureTerminal lists the company in Columbus, Ohio.

The Technology

Atlas Atomics is developing an improved heavy water reactor. Unlike most reactors operating in the US, heavy water designs can run on natural uranium rather than enriched uranium. That matters because enrichment is expensive and global capacity is concentrated in a handful of suppliers, with Russia historically among the largest.

Avoiding enrichment could make Atlas's reactors cheaper to fuel and less exposed to supply bottlenecks. In a letter to Utah's Governor's Office of Energy Development, Gan said the technology aims to provide reliable power, expand production of medical and industrial isotopes and support nuclear fuel recycling.

Why It Matters

A $400 million Series A is one of the largest early-stage rounds in nuclear energy, and it arrives as demand for round-the-clock, carbon-free power climbs, driven largely by AI data centers. Tech companies have signed deals to restart old reactors and back new designs, and investors have followed with large checks into advanced nuclear startups.

Heavy water reactors are not new. Canada's CANDU fleet has run on the approach for decades. That track record could help with regulators, though any new design still faces a long licensing process with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. For Ohio, the company's ties to the state add to a growing presence in energy and advanced manufacturing investment.

Valuing a stealth company at nearly $2 billion before it has publicly shown a reactor is a large bet on its team. With a former Oak Ridge executive running the nuclear program and two of venture capital's biggest firms behind it, Atlas Atomics has the money and credibility to make its case.

item.title: Can Light Beat Nvidia? Volantis Raises $88M for Photonic AI Chips
item.dc:creator: YourInfoDaily
item.description: Volantis raised an $88M Series A co-led by Lachy Groom and Abstract Ventures to build photonic AI inference systems that break the memory wall.
item.content:encoded:
Backed by Lachy Groom, Abstract Ventures and John Doerr, the San Francisco startup is using light to break the memory bottleneck in AI hardware.

Volantis, a San Francisco semiconductor company building AI inference systems that move data with light, has raised an $88 million Series A co-led by Lachy Groom and Abstract Ventures. The company announced the round as it works toward delivering its first integrated inference engines in 2027.

John Doerr, VXI Capital, Triatomic and Susa Ventures also invested, along with angel investors Dwarkesh Patel, Naveen Rao and Sholto Douglas.

WHAT VOLANTIS IS BUILDING

Volantis is going after what chip designers call the memory wall. As AI models grow, the limiting factor in running them is often not how fast a processor can compute but how quickly data can travel between the processor and memory. Electrical connections can only carry so much, and that ceiling restricts both model size and response speed.

The company's answer is photonics, using light in place of electrical signals to connect chips to memory. Its first system, called A-1, combines custom micro-VCSELs, a type of very small laser, with photonic interconnects designed specifically for chip-to-memory links.

Volantis says the architecture will let models exceeding 20 trillion parameters run at up to 10,000 tokens per second per user while lowering the cost of inference. Those are company targets for a system that has not yet shipped, and they would represent a substantial leap over what current hardware delivers.

THE TEAM BEHIND VOLANTIS

Volantis is led by CEO and co-founder Tapa Ghosh. The team includes veterans of NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and Ayar Labs, with experience spanning CoWoS advanced packaging products, tunable VCSELs and silicon photonics systems.

"Today's hardware forces a tradeoff between running the largest models and running them fast. We started Volantis to eliminate that tradeoff," Ghosh said in the announcement.

HOW VOLANTIS WILL USE THE $88M

The funding will go toward developing and commercializing A-1, expanding the engineering team and preparing for customer deployments. The company is targeting 2027 for delivery of its first integrated inference engines.

An $88 million Series A is large by most standards but in line with what chip startups require. Designing, fabricating and packaging custom silicon and optics is capital intensive well before any revenue arrives.

WHY THE VOLANTIS FUNDING MATTERS

Most attention in AI hardware has centered on training, the process of building models. Inference, the work of running them for users, is where spending is shifting as AI products reach large audiences. Each query carries a cost, and that cost determines which products are viable.

Hardware that serves larger models faster and more cheaply would change that math. It is why investors continue to fund alternatives to conventional GPU systems, and why photonics, long confined to networking between servers, is now being pushed closer to the chip.

The investor list reflects that conviction. Doerr is one of Silicon Valley's best-known venture investors, Rao has founded AI chip companies of his own, and Patel and Douglas are closely followed voices in AI research circles.

Volantis still has to prove its design in production silicon. If A-1 performs as described, it would give AI developers a new way around one of the hardest constraints in the field.
